idiom_name: java.util.ServiceLoader typed provider registry (reload() clears the binding cache)
implementation_notes: ServiceLoader is the JVM's provider registry: ServiceLoader.load(CodecFactory.class) locates implementations declared in META-INF/services/<service> on the class path or in `provides` directives on the module path, instantiates them lazily and caches the providers it has loaded. What replaces the classic structure is the service interface acting as the name plus the provider configuration acting as the binding, so application code iterates or streams providers and never names a location. Re-resolution is explicit: reload() drops the cached providers so the next iteration rediscovers them, which is the hook to call after a plugin set changes.
pitfalls: Providers load lazily, so ServiceConfigurationError can surface in the middle of iteration; handle it around the whole traversal, not around load().
A long-lived loader keeps the provider set from its first iteration; without reload() a newly deployed provider is invisible and a removed one still resolves.
On the module path a provider must be public, must not be an inner class, and needs either a public no-argument constructor or a static provider() method; violations appear only at resolution time.

variants.name: JNDI naming/directory lookup (Context.lookup)
variants.idiom_name: InitialContext.lookup(name) against a naming or directory service
variants.implementation_notes: The classic naming-service realization: an InitialContext bound to a provider (LDAP, DNS, RMI, COS naming, file system) resolves a compound name to the object bound to it via Context.lookup(name), while listBindings/list enumerate the available bindings. The container or administrator owns the bindings, so moving a resource means rebinding the name and client code keeps the same lookup call; the provider plug-in mechanism lets one API span different directory technologies. Choose it when resources are managed outside the application (application-server data sources, JMS destinations) or when the registry must be shared across processes.
pitfalls: JNDI names are provider- and environment-specific: java:comp/env/... only exists inside a Java EE container, while ldap:/// names couple the code to the directory layout.
lookup() throws NamingException both for a missing binding (NameNotFound) and for an unreachable service - retry the latter with backoff, never the former.
Contexts hold provider connections and must be closed; leaking them exhausts the directory server's connection pool.
